la:noun:tribunus.html:
trĭbūnus, i, m.
tribus, prop. the chief of a tribe; hence, in gen.
,
a chieftain, commander, tribune.
Tribuni aerarii, paymasters, who assisted the quaestors, Cato ap. ; cf. Müll.; ib.; called also tribuni aeris,. By the Lex Aurelia these tribuni aerarii were made judges on the part of the people: (Milonem) tribuni aerarii condemnarunt,; : a tribunis aerariis absolutus,; cf. in a pun with aerati (rich),. This judicial office was taken from them by Julius Cæsar, .—
Tribuni Celerum, captains or commanders of the Celeres, ; cf. ; Weissenb. ad . —
Tribuni militares or militum, tribunes of the soldiers, military tribunes; these were officers of the army, six to each legion, who commanded in turn, each two months at a time: qui M. Aemilio legati et praefecti et tribuni militares fuerunt,; so, militares,; cf. in sing.: cum tribunus militaris depugnavi apud Thermopylas,: a tribunis militum, praefectis reliquisque, qui, etc.,; so, militum,; cf. in sing.: tribunus militum,; : tribuni cohortium,.—Sing.: Stilonius Priscus qui tribunus cohortis, sub Classico fuerat,; cf.: tribunus minor,; and tribunus legionis,.—
Tribuni militum consulari potestate, military tribunes with consular power; these were the highest officers of the State from A.U.C. 310 to A.U.C. 388. They were chosen from the patrician and plebeian orders, and were at first three, then six, and, after the year 352, eight in number, ; ; ; called tribuni consulares,; Becker, Antiq. 2, 2, p. 136 sq.—
Tribuni plebis, and more freq. simply tribuni, tribunes of the people, whose office it was to defend the rights and interests of the Roman plebeians against the encroachments of the patricians, ; sq.; ; ; cf. Becker, Antiq. 2, 2, p. 247 sq.; Lange, Antiq. 1, 1, p. 592 sq., and the authorities cited by both.

la:noun:triduum.gloss: the space of three days, three days
senses: the space of three days, three days
la:noun:triduum.html:
trīdŭum, i, n. (sc. spatium) [tres-dies],
the space of three days, three days: ubi triduom continuom,: hanc hoc triduom solum sinas Esse hic,: triduom servire numquam te sinam,: bidui'st aut tridui Haec sollicitudo?: ut maneas triduom hoc,: decrevit habendas triduum ferias,: cum tridui viam processisset,: Clodius respondit, triduo illum, ad summum quatriduo periturum,: triduo intermisso,; ; ; .

la:noun:tribunatus.html:
trĭbūnātus, ūs, m.
id.
,
the office and dignity of a tribune, the tribuneship: Cotta, qui tribunatum plebis petebat,; ; so of the office of a tribune of the people, ; ; ; ; ; ; ; .— Of a military tribune: tribunatus commoda contemnere,; ; . 30, 31, § 113.

la:noun:tribus.gloss: One of the three original tribes of Rome: Ramnes, Tities, Luceres.
senses: One of the three original tribes of Rome: Ramnes, Tities, Luceres.
A division of the Roman people.
la:noun:tribus.html:
trĭbus, ūs (dat. and
abl. plur.: tribubus,; ; , etc.; but trebibos, Ephem. Epigr. 2, 208, n. 299; never tribibus; cf. , and v., in gen., Neue, Formenl. 1, 361 sqq.), f.
tri-; root in tres (dat. tribus) and bhū; Gr. φυ- in φυλή; v. Corss. Ausspr. 1, 163
, orig. a third part of the Roman people; as their numbers increased it came to mean,
Lit., a division of the people, a tribe (the number of these tribes finally increased to thirty-five, of which thirty-one were rusticae tribus or country tribes, and four urbanae tribus or city tribes; the following are the names of the tribes, the city tribes being printed in Italics, viz.: Aemilia, Aniensis, Arniensis, Claudia, Collina, Cornelia, Crustumina, Esquilina, Fabia, Falerina, Galesia, Horatia, Lemonia, Maecia, Menenia, Oufentina, Palatina, Papiria, Pollia, Pomptina, Popilia, Pupinia, Quirina, Romilia, Sabatina, Scaptia, Sergia, Stellatina, Suburana, Terentina, Tromentina, Veientina, Velina, Veturia, Voltinia. Some of these names are the same as the names of Roman gentes, and others are derived from the names of places where these tribes at first resided), ; ; ; ; Weissenb. ad loc.; ; ; ; ; cf. Niebuhr, Röm. Gesch. 1, p. 426 sq.; and see the names of these tribes in Inscr. Orell. II. pp. 11-28 and 147: inventum tamen esse fortem amicum ex eādem familia Q. Verrem Romilia,of the Romilian tribe,; cf. Ser. Sulpicius, Q. F. Lemonia, Rufus,: L. AVRELIVS L. FIL. CAMILIA FIRMVS, etc.,: Africanus censor tribu movebat eum centurionem, qui in Pauli pugna non affuerat,removed, expelled from the tribe,; so, tribu movere aliquem,; ; ; ; 45, 15, 4; : urbanae (tribus) in quas transferri ignominia esset, desidiae probro,: populus in tribus convocatus,: ea multitudo tribus circuit, genibus se omnium advolvens,.—
Trop., comicè: grammaticas ambire tribus,to canvass the Grammarian tribe,.—
Transf.
Of Macedonians: satellites illi ex tribu suā legunt, (al. turbā).—
In gen., the commonalty, the mass, mob, poor people, ; : equitem imitatae tribus,. — Prov.: sine tribu, without rank or position: homo sine tribu, sine nomine,.

senses: to yield, give up, concede, allow
la:verb:tribuo.html:
trĭbŭo, ŭi, ūtum, 3, v. a.
tribus
,
to assign, impart, allot, bestow, give, etc. (syn.: do, dono, largior).
Lit.: ut ei plurimum tribuamus, a quo plurimum deligimur,: in tribuendo suum cuique,: si uni omnia tribuenda sint,: praemia alicui,; ; : cujus sceleribus tanta praemia tribuistis, Dietsch: dona nulli,; : beneficia,: pretium aedium Aurelio,: pecunias ex modo detrimenti,to deal out, allot,. —
Trop.
In gen., to grant, give, show, pay, render: misericordiam fortissimo viro,; so, veniam alicui,: inventoribus gratiam,: silentium orationi alicujus,: quod tantum dignitatis civitati Aeduae tribuerat,; cf.: sibi honorem,: mulieri honorem,: tibi turis honorem,: vocabula monti,: salutem mihi, (16), 2: parem voluntatem paribus beneficiis,: pacem terris,; et saep. —
In partic.
Pregn., to grant, yield, give up, concede, allow something to a person or thing (syn. concedo): si sit quispiam, qui aliquid tribuat voluptati,: valetudini aliquid,: observantiam officio, non timori neque spei,: hoc matris precibus,: aliquid rei publicae et amicitiae,: ego tantum tibi tribuo, quantum mihi fortasse arrogo, I yield or concede as much to you, have as high an opinion of you, : cum senatus impediretur quo minus, id quod hostibus semper erat tributum, responsum equitibus Romanis redderetur,; cf.: gratissimum mihi feceris, si huic commendationi meae tantum tribueris quantum cui tribuisti plurimum,; and: nusquam tantum tribuitur aetati (quam Lacedaemone),: mihi tribuebat omnia,gave me the preference in all things, deferred in every thing to me,.—Absol.: cum universo ordini publicanorum semper libentissime tribuerim,: quos ne nominatim tradam, majoribus eorum tribuendum puto,: tribus in generibus rerum versari rhetoris officium ... demonstrativum est, quod tribuitur in alicujus certae personae laudem aut vituperationem,. —
To ascribe, assign, attribute a thing to a person or thing as the cause: aliquid virtuti hostium,: aliquid juri potius quam suae culpae,: id tribuite vestrae culpae,: aliquid ignaviae,: miseriae nostrae potius quam inconstantiae tribuere quod, etc.,—
To set store by, with magnopere, multum, etc., to make much of: quibus ille secundum fratrem plurimum tribuebat,: ne ob eam rem suae magnopere virtuti tribueret,.—
To divide, distribute (syn. dispertio): rem universam in partes,; : secundus (locus) in tempora tribuitur,: omnem vim loquendi in duas partes,.—
Of time, to bestow or spend upon, devote to a thing: comitiis omnibus perficiundis XI. dies tribuit,: his rebus tantum temporis tribuit,: reliqua tempora litteris,; .—Hence, trĭbūtum, i, n., a stated payment, a contribution, tribute.
Lit. (class.): in capita singula servorum et liberorum tributum imponebatur,: a se intolerabilia tributa exigi,: omnes Siculi ex censu quotannis tributa conferunt,: tributa pendere,: ceram in tributa praestare,: civitates tributis liberare,: tributo populo indicto,: imperare,; ; ; ; ; ; ; .—In the ante-class. collat. form trĭbūtus, i, m.: cum tributus exigeretur, Cato ap. : tributus cum imperatus est,—
Transf.
A contribution made for any private purpose (jurid. Lat.), ; ; .—
A gift, present (poet.): Saturnalicium,: praestare tributa clientes cogimur,; .

la:noun:Triarius.html:
Trĭārĭus, ii, m.,
a surname in the gens Valeria.
C. Valerius Triarius, a friend of Cicero, ; he is introduced as a speaker in Cicero's treatise de Finibus; v. —
His father was named L. Valerius Triarius, .—
P. Valerius Triarius, the accuser of M. Scaurus, ; .

la:num:triginta.html:
trīginta (freq. written
), num. adj. indecl. [τριάκοντα], thirty: minae,: Romulus cum septem et triginta regnavisset annos,; : triginta magnos orbīs explebit,: conjectus in carcerem triginta jussu tyrannorum,of the thirty tyrants (in Athens), ; cf. ; ; Mos. N. cr.

la:noun:tristitia.html:
tristĭtĭa, ae, f.
id.
,
sadness, mournfulness, sorrow, grief, melancholy, gloominess, dejection (class.; syn. maestitia).
In gen.
Of living beings: tum ad tristitiam, tum ad laetitiam est contorquendus,: ex summā laetitiā atque lasciviā repente omnes tristitia invasit,: in eādem tristitiā permanere,: magno metu ac tristitiā sollicitari, Auct. B. Afr. 10: lacrimis ac tristitiā te tradidisti, Luccei. ap. : tu sapiens finire memento Tristitiam,: tristitiam compescere,: esse aliquam cognatam tristitiae voluptatem,: (vino) tristitia et cura hebetatur,: tristitiam animi resolvi,: subitā tristitiā implicatis militum animis,: cum tristitiā et maerore in vitā remanere,: tristitiam ad ultimam perductus,.— Trop.: sol recedens quasi tristitiā quādam contrahit terram,.—
Of things: haec tristitia temporum,this sad state of the times,: caeli,: indurata soli,: aspectus,: lenitate verbi rei tristitiam mitigare,hardness, harshness,.—
In partic., of demeanor, moroseness, sourness, gloominess, harshness, sternness, severity, etc. (syn. severitas): an nova tristitiae causa puella tuae?: simque ego tristitiae causa modusque tuae,: (risus) tristitiam ac severitatem mitigat, relaxat,; cf. : illorum (philosophorum) tristitiam atque asperitatem fugiens,: quod ille vos tristitiā vultuque deceperit,; so prooem. § 15: non conveniant barbae illi atque tristitiae,; ; ; ; .

la:adj:triplex.html:
trī^plex, ĭcis (abl. regularly triplici;
triplice,; Ven. Carm. 7, 4, 12), adj.
ter-plico
, threefold, triple.
Lit.
Adj.: Plato triplicem finxit animum,: philosophandi ratio triplex,: nec me pastoris Iberi Forma triplex, nec forma triplex tua, Cerbere, movit, Ov M. 9, 185: cuspis, i. e. Neptune's trident, : mundus (because made up of sky, land, and sea),: regnum (because shared among Jupiter, Neptune, and Pluto),: vultus Dianae (because also Luna and Hecate; v. triceps and triformis),: triplicem aciem instruere, to draw up an army in three lines or columns, to form a triple line, ; so, acies,; ; ; cf. comically: paravi copias duplices, triplices dolos. perfidias,: vallus, Auct. B. Alex. 2, 3: murus,; : aes,; : triplici stant ordine dentes, et saep. — Poet., of three like persons or things belonging together: triplices Sorores,

the three sisters, i. e. the Fates, ; called triplices deae,; cf.: quae ratum triplici pollice netis opus,i. e. the finger of the three Fates,: poenarum deae triplices, i. e. the Furies, id. M, 8, 481: Minyeïdes,i. e. the three daughters of Minyas,: greges,three bands of Bacchantes, (4, 16), 24; cf. gens,three clans,. —

Substt.
trī^plex, ĭcis, n., three times as much, a threefold portion, triple: sume tibi decies; tibi tantundem; tibi triplex, 3, 237; cf.: pediti in singulos dati centeni (denarii), duplex centurioni, triplex equiti,; : olei veteris triplex adicitur,. —
trī^plĭces, ĭum, m. (sc. codicilli), a writing-tablet with three leaves, ; ; ; .—*
Transf., very great or strong: triplici fluctu, ap. ( Dietsch). — Adv.: trĭplĭcĭ-ter, in a threefold manner, in three ways: commutare,: l littera tripliciter sonat, .

la:adj:tristis.html:
tristis, e, adj.
etym. dub.; cf. Sanscr. trastas, frightened; and Lat. terreo
,
sad, sorrowful, mournful, dejected, melancholy, disconsolate, trist (syn.: maestus, severus, austerus, luctuosus).
In gen.: maesti tristesque,: cum maestus errares, quaerere ex te, quid tristis esses,: tristis et conturbatus,: tristis, demissus,: sic tristes affatus amicos,: Sequanos tristes, capite demisso, terram intueri,: numquam ego te tristiorem Vidi esse,: oderunt hilarem tristes, tristemque jocosi,: (faciet) hominem ex tristi lepidum et lenem,: quid tu tristis es?; ; : quid es tam tristis?: malle se adulescentem tristem quam hilarem,: tristis Erat et me maestum videbat,; .—
Transf.
Of things associated with misfortune or suggestive of sadness, melancholy, saddening, unhappy: ut tuum laetissimum diem cum tristissimo meo conferam,; cf.: vel defensus tristibus temporibus vel ornatus secundis,: esse vultu tristi,: tristissima exta,: tristissimi exsilii solatium,: tristissimam exegimus noctem,most miserable,: sors,unhappy, miserable,: eventus,: Kalendae,sad, dismal,: Hyades,: Orion,: bella,: clades,: morbus,: fatum,: jus sepulcri,: officium (exsequiarum),: funera,; : pars subiere feretro, Triste ministerium,: Tartara,: Acheron,: tristique palus inamabilis undā,; : arbores,gloomy, sombre,: adspectus (arboris),: tristes et squalidi trunci,.—
Of taste: quod triste et amarum est,harsh, disagreeable, bitter,: suci,: lupinum,: absinthia,; : epulae,: sapor. : pocula,.—
Of smell, offensive, foul: anhelitus oris,.—
As subst.: triste, is, n., a sad thing, etc. (poet.): triste lupus stabulis, maturis frugibus imbres, Arboribus venti,a sad thing, a pest, bane,: interdum miscentur tristia laetis,; cf.: nunc ego mitibus Mutare quaero tristia,. Thus Ovid called his elegies that were written in exile Tristia.—
In partic.
Of behavior, etc., towards others.
Glum, gloomy, peevish, morose, ill-humored (syn.: tetricus, severus, austerus): stultitia est, ei te esse tristem,: eia, mea Juno, non decet te esse tam

tristem tuo Jovi, : mihi erit tristior, Afran. ap. : tristis amica ingrato viro,: puella,: navita tristis (Charon),gloomy, sullen,; so, dii,: Erinys,: sorores,i. e. the Fates,; : ursa,.—

Stern, harsh, severe: judex tristis et integer,; cf.: cum tristibus severe, cum remissis jucunde vivere,.—
Transf., of things, gloomy, sad, melancholy, stern, harsh, etc.: truculentis oculis, tristi fronte,: voltus,: fronte gravi et tristi supercilio,: idem naturā tristiori paululo, Afran. ap. : vultus severior et tristior,; cf.: tristis severitas inest in vultu,: vita tristior,: triste et severum genus dicendi,; cf.: sermo tristis (opp. jocosus),: senectus, Verg. ap. ; cf.: tristis et plenus dignitatis sonus,: perfert in judiciis tristem et impexam antiquitatem,.—Of languages, etc.: tua tristia dicta,: sententia,; : responsum,: senatūs consultum,.— Adv.: tristĕ, sadly, sorrowfully; harshly, severely: salutantes,: triste et acutum resonare,: rigens frons,.—Comp.: flere tristius, (3, 13), 2: adulescentes gravius aegrotant, tristius curantur,with more difficulty,: respondere tristius,more harshly,.

la:noun:triens.html:
trĭens, entis, m.
tres
,
a third part, a third of any thing.
In gen.: cum sciemus, quantum quasi sit in trientis triente,: medicaminis,: ut triens ex heminā supersit,.—Of inheritances: cum duobus coheredibus esse in triente,: heredes ex triente,.—
In partic.
Of coins.
The third part of an as, Müll.; ; ; ; ; Messala ap. ; .—
Under the later emperors, a gold coin, the third part of an aureus, Gall. ap. Treb. —
As a measure of interest, one third per cent. monthly, or, in our way of reckoning, four per cent. yearly: usurae,: pensiones,.—
In square or long measure.
The third of a juger, ; .—
The third of a foot in length, ; . —
In liquid measure, a third of a sextarius, i. e. four cyathi, (4, 9), 29; ; ; ; 10, 49, 1.—
Among mathematicians, the number two (as a third of six), —
Trientem tertium ... id significare ait Cincius duas libras pondo et trientem, .

trīclīnĭum, ii, n., = τρικλίνιον,

Lit.: triclinio posito cenabimus,: sternere, Müll.: habueris quinquaginta tricliniorum lectos,: in triclinio, quod in foro straverat,, § 61; ; and 2; ; —

la:noun:triumphus.gloss: a hymn in honor of Bacchus (translating Greek θρίαμβος (thríambos))
senses: a hymn in honor of Bacchus (translating Greek θρίαμβος (thríambos))
triumpe (a ritual exclamation of the Arval Brothers)
the Roman Triumph (a ceremonial procession in celebration of a military victory)
la:noun:triumphus.html:
triumphus (in the earliest per. written triumpus;
v.the foll.; and cf. ; ; and the letter P), i, m.
cf. θρίαμβος, a hymn in honor of Bacchus
.
TRIVMPE, an exclamation used in the solemn processions of the Arval brothers: ENOS MARMOR IVVATO. TRIVMPE, TRIVMPE, TRIVMPE, Carm. Fratr. Arv. ap. .—
A solemn and magnificent entrance of a general into Rome after having obtained an important victory, a triumphal procession, triumph (cf. Smith, Antiq. 1163 sqq.): disseres de triumpho. Quid tandem habet iste currus? quid vincti ante currum duces! quid simulacra oppidorum? quid aurum? etc.,; cf. ; cf. : triumphum deportare,: ne in triumpho duceretur,: Gallos Caesar in triumphum ducit,: senatus cum triumphum Africano decerneret,: de classe populi Romani triumphum agere,; : triumphum ex Etruriā agere,: deportare triumphum ex provinciā, : Boiorum triumphi spem collegae reliquit,for a victory over the Boii,; cf.: Pharsalicae pugnae ne triumphum quidem egit,: per triumphum aliquem ducere,; Dietsch: triumpho clarissimo urbem est invectus,: elephantos ducere in triumpho,: (res) justissimi triumphi, i. e. worthy of a triumph, Vatin. ap. : qui (Pompeius) tot habet triumphos, quot orae sunt partesque terrarum,: albi greges ... Romanos ad templa deūm duxere triumphos,i. e. were carried before the processions,.—The shout of the soldiery and the multitude on occasion of these triumphal processions was: Io triumphe, and 50; ; ; cf. ; ; .—
Trop., a triumph, victory: ut repulsam tuam triumphum suum duxerint,: luxuriae (gen. subj.), : de se ipso,.

[triginta], the thirtieth: idem tricesimo post die feci,: tertius et tricesimus annus,: sexto tricesimo anno post,: legio quinta tricesima, Galb. ap. : tricesimo sexto anno,: tricesimum annum agens,: tricesimo die,: tricesima sabbata,: bis trigesimus consul instat,. — Hence, subst.: Trīcēsĭmae, ārum, f., the name of a town in Gallia Belgica on the Rhine, .

trĭennĭum, ii, n. (sc. spatium) [id.],

la:noun:tribunal.gloss: a raised semicircular or square platform, on which the seats of magistrates were placed; tribunal, judgment seat, dais, camp platform
senses: a raised semicircular or square platform, on which the seats of magistrates were placed; tribunal, judgment seat, dais, camp platform
a court of law, tribunal; judgment
any platform used for purposes other than above
la:noun:tribunal.html:
trĭbūnal (moleste diligentibus permittamus et tribunale dicere, ; yet trĭbūnāle is found Corp. Inscr. Lat. 206, 24), ālis, n.
tribunus
.
Lit.
A raised semicircular or square platform, on which the seats of magistrates were placed, a judgment-seat, tribunal (cf.: suggestus, sella): compleatur tribunal,: popularis accessus ac tribunal,: praetor tribunal suum juxta Trebonii praetoris urbani sellam collocavit,; cf. ; : eum de tribunali deturbavit,; : (praetor) palam de sellā ac tribunali pronuntiat, Si quis, etc.,: quem ad se vocari et de tribunali citari jussit,, § 16: pro tribunali agere aliquid,; cf. : qui dicunt apud tribunalia,; cf. : laudatum ex quattuor tribu nalibus,: nobis in tribunali praetoris urbani sedentibus,: sedens pro tribunali,: Fulvius magnā circumfusus turbā ad tribunal consulis venit,; cf. .—
The elevation in the camp, from which the general addressed the soldiers or administered justice, ; ; ; cf.: regium (sc. Porsenae),.—
The seat of the prætor in the theatre, .—
A tribunal erected as a monument to a deceased person of high rank: sepulcrum Antiochiae ubi crematus (Germanicus), tribunal Epidaphnae, quo in loco vitam finierat,; .—
Transf., in gen., a mound, dam, embankment: tribunalia structa manibus ad experimenta altissimi aestūs,.—
Of the persons who sit on a tribunal, the magistrates: omne forum quem spectat et omne tribunal,.—
Trop., height, greatness: quid superest ad honoris mei tribunal et columen, ad laudis meae cumulum?.

trĭumpho, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a.

[triumphus].

Neutr., to make a triumphal procession, to hold or celebrate a triumph, to triumph (cf. ovo).
Lit.: triumphare appellatum, quod cum imperatore milites redeuntes clamitant per urbem in Capitolium eunti Io triumphe: id a θριάμβῳ Graeco Liberi cognomento potest dictum, Müll.: ex praeturā triumphare,: commissi sunt iis magistratus, in quibus re bene gestā triumpharent,: Africanus, qui de Numantinis triumpharat,; for which: ex Transalpinis gentibus triumpharunt,: ex Macedoniā,; : ex Transalpinis bellis,: cum triumphantem (Camillum) albi per urbem vexerant equi,: ut triumphanti urbem inire liceret,: quasi debellato triumphare,: neminem ad eam diem triumphasse, qui, etc.,: quid tam inauditum quam equitem Romanum triumphare? at Pompeius triumphavit,: nisi meo in rem publicam beneficio ubi triumpharet esset habiturus,; cf. Auct. B. Afr. 22, 3: Nero ovans triumphavit, i. e. held or celebrated an ovation, . —Poet., transf.: ut sit mulsum, qui triumphent milites,: mirum, si de me jure triumphat Amor, (8, b), 40 (24): deque cothurnato vate triumphat Amor,.— Impers. pass.: ex eā urbe triumphari vidimus,: aliquis est Romae, qui triumphari de Macedonibus nolit?: populi jussu triumphatum est,: de parvis oppidis,: ex civilibus bellis,.—
Trop., to triumph, exult, be glad, rejoice exceedingly: exsultare laetitiā, triumphare gaudio,; cf.: laetaris tu in omnium gemitu et triumphas,: in quo exsultat et triumphat oratio mea,: triumpho, si licet me, etc.,: meum factum probari abs te, triumpho gaudio, Caes. ap. .—
Act. (only poet. and in post-Aug. prose).
With a homogeneous object: triumphavit cum imperatoribus suis triumphos novem,.—More freq.,
With other objects, to triumph over, to lead in triumph; or, in gen., to conquer: aliquem, Treb. XXX. Tyr. 24: hic terram triumphabit,: mortem Cum suis terroribus,; .—More freq. in pass.: bisque triumphatas utroque ab litore gentes,: triumphatis dare jura Medis,: Zenobia victa et triumphata,: triumphati magis quam victi sunt,: triumphata Capitolia,; cf.: omnia superata et triumphata,: ne triumpharetur (Mithridates),: Roma triumphati caput orbis,: triumphatus bos, i. e. obtained by victory, got or won as booty, ; so, triumphatum aurum,: Achaeos triumphandos Mummio tradidit,.—Hence, p. a.: trĭ-umphans, antis, = triumphalis, triumphal, belonging to a triumph: equi,.

la:noun:tripudium.html:
trĭpŭdĭum, ii, n.
acc. to , contr. from terripavium, terripudium, but prob. from ter and pes; cf. the old form tripodare, whence tripodatio
; in relig. lang.,
Lit., a measured stamping, a leaping, jumping, dancing in relig. solemnities, a solemn religious dance: Salios ancilia ferre ac per urbem ire canentes carmina, cum tripudiis sollemnique saltatu jussit,; cf. tripudio and † tripodatio.—
Transf., in gen., a dance: citatis celerare tripudiis,: tripudia Hispanorum,: cum sui moris tripudiis,: cantus incohantium proelium et ululatus et tripudia,.—
A favorable omen, when the sacred chickens ate so greedily that the food dropped from their mouths to the ground, ; ; ; ; ; cf. solistimus.
